extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and students of poetics (writers of tragedy and epic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama and epic narrative: structure, plot devices (peripety, discovery), diction, use of metre, plausibility/marvellous, and the role of the chorus and spectacle. Emphasizes unity, appropriate length, and stylistic balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (single action, organic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of stories should be based on a single action, one that is a complete whole in itself, with a beginning, middle, and end, so as to enable the work to produce its own proper pleasure with all the organic unity of a living creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making a work out of multiple, disconnected actions or merely a period of events; an epic or drama should enable the beginning and end to be taken in at one view. Unity is the primary ground on which two tragedies are judged the same or not (same Complication and Denouement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Length (beginning and end viewable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem/play must be of such length that its beginning and end can be taken in at one view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic length should be shorter than the oldest epics and about as long as a series of tragedies offered for one hearing. Do not dramatize an entire epic-body of incident (e.g., the whole Iliad) — that scale ruins dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as Complication and Denouement (structure mastery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication (all up to the change in hero's fortunes) and in part Denouement (from the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing plots, assess whether Complication and Denouement match. Many dramatists succeed in Complication but fail in Denouement; both must be mastered. Complication includes presupposed incidents as well as those before opening scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety and Discovery (core constituents for complex plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex tragedy consists essentially of Peripety (reversal) and Discovery (recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are central to creating the tragic effect; combining them successfully defines the 'complex' species of tragedy and produces powerful emotional shifts in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four species of Tragedy and combining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four distinct species: (1) complex (all Peripety and Discovery), (2) tragedy of suffering, (3) tragedy of character, (4) spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should, if possible, combine every element of interest or at least the more important ones; critics often unfairly expect one poet to excel in all specific strengths of predecessors, so aim to include the major parts rather than only isolated strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and take a share in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a Chorus that participates in the plot (Sophoclean model) rather than one whose songs are merely intercalary and unrelated (later practice introduced by Agathon). Avoid the anti-pattern of inserting songs that do not move the action forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Thought: Thought revealed by language and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (the ideas and aims of characters) is shown in everything effected by their language and must align with their actions; spoken words must produce the intended impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought belongs to rhetoric, but in drama it must be consistent across speech and deed. Actions should have the same mental procedure as speech when arousing pity, fear, or other emotions — action makes impressions without explanation, words must produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction should be clear and not mean (balance ordinary and unfamiliar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of Diction is for it to be at once clear and not mean: ordinary words give clearness; unfamiliar terms (strange words, metaphors, lengthened/curtailed forms) give distinction and non-prosaic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a measured admixture: too many metaphors produce riddles; too many strange words produce barbarisms. Lengthened/curtailed/altered forms can give non-prosaic color while remaining recognizably clear. Moderation is essential — overuse invites ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place elaborate diction only where no action/character/thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate diction is required only in places where there is no action and no Character or Thought to be revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Character or Thought is present, over-ornate diction tends to obscure them. Test ornate phrases by substituting ordinary words to check whether the diction truly improves the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Metaphor (highest poetic skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to be a master of metaphor; a good metaphor implies an intuitive perception of the similarity in dissimilars and is a sign of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor cannot be fully learned by imitation; it should be used where it reveals a real likeness. Qualified metaphors (adding what the word supplants is relative, or negating an attribute) are stylistic devices illustrated in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and types of non-ordinary word-forms (coinages, lengthening, curtailing, alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be ordinary, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, coined, lengthened out, curtailed, or altered in form; these devices affect tone and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coined/strange words and altered forms can add distinction but risk barbarism if overused. Lengthened/curtailed forms can give a non-prosaic appearance while keeping intelligibility. Apply moderation and test by replacing with ordinary words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate vocabulary and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres allow different word-kinds: compounds most fitting in dithyramb, strange words in heroic, metaphors in iambic; heroic may avail itself of them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iambic, modeling spoken language, should restrict itself mainly to ordinary words, metaphor, and ornamental equivalent. Choose vocabulary according to metrical and genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter suitability (heroic for epic; metre must fit genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry has heroic metre assigned by experience; other metres would be incongruous for long narrative poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metre appropriate to the story's gravitas: heroic is weighty and tolerates strange words and metaphors; iambic and trochaic connote movement/action or dance and are less suitable for long epic narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dramatize an epic body of incident (avoid plurality-of-stories in drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not write a tragedy on an epic body of incident (i.e., one with plurality of stories) by attempting to dramatize the entire story (e.g., whole Iliad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic scale treats many parts at length; drama concentrating that same material tends to be disappointing. Successful dramatizations take parts or episodes (e.g., Euripides, Aeschylus) rather than trying to stage the full epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode use: permissible in epic, damaging in drama if excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes in epic relieve uniformity and can be used to increase grandeur and variety; in drama, episodic plurality undermines unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In epic, simultaneous and diverse incidents can enrich the poem; in drama, maintain concentrated action to avoid satiety and loss of tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvellous and Probability: prefer convincing impossibility to unconvincing possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous is required in Tragedy; epic affords more opening for the improbable. A likely impossibility is always preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improbable incidents are necessary, keep them outside the piece (e.g., prior events) rather than making them internal; conceal or justify improbabilities by other excellences; but unnecessary improbability or avoidable absurdities are faults of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling critics' objections (five fault-classes and methods of rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms typically allege something is (1) impossible, (2) improbable, (3) corrupting, (4) contradictory, or (5) against technical correctness. Solutions must be sought under established heads (e.g., justify by poetry's requirements, by opinion, or by reference to custom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify impossibilities if they serve poetic ends; argue improbabilities by appeal to opinion or probability against probability; resolve contradictions by close dialectical parsing (sense, relation, punctuation, equivocal terms, custom of language, metaphor, or reinterpretation). There is no apology for avoidable improbability of plot or depravity of character when unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's role in narrative: minimal overt intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should say very little in propria persona; he is no imitator when doing that and should promptly bring in characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer is praised for brief preface and then introducing fully characterized persons. Excessive poetial intrusion undermines imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic must include same parts as Tragedy (except Song and Spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must divide into the same species as Tragedy: simple or complex, character or suffering; parts (Peripeties, Discoveries, scenes of suffering) must be present except Song and Spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic differs mainly in length and metre, but structurally it requires the same essential elements; assess epic on presence and handling of peripety, discovery and suffering scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration vs breadth: Tragedy's advantage in focused effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy requires less space for its end and yields a more concentrated, pleasurable effect than expansive epic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate the work's economy of means: a concentrated tragic imitation (e.g., Oedipus) can be more effective than an expanded epic-scale treatment; avoid diluting tragic impact by unnecessary expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of linguistic/lexical solutions to apparent errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent faults (odd words, contradictions, improbabilities) may be resolved by assuming strange words, metaphorical senses, alternate punctuation/reading, equivocal terms, or appeal to linguistic/customary usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning a poet for contradiction or impossibility, test multiple readings and linguistic explanations; many Homeric difficulties may be solved by such philological devices. However, technical errors directly in matters relevant to the depicted art/knowledge (e.g., medicine) are more serious than poetic license.
